passage: At the sports club's annual trip, a few older boys went behind the bus at the rest stop. Zubin followed out of curiosity. One of them held out a vape. "Try it, it's just flavour." Zubin hesitated. His coach had talked about how it can hook people quickly and hurt breathing. His teammate Jahnavi came around the bus just then, looking for him. Zubin said, loud enough, "Nah, I've got the match tomorrow. I need my lungs." The older boy shrugged. "Your loss." Jahnavi said, "Come on, the bus is leaving." Back on the bus, Zubin's heart was still racing. "Did I sound stupid?" he asked. Jahnavi grinned. "You sounded like someone who wants to win."

qa.q: What reason did Zubin give for saying no?
qa.a: He said he had a match tomorrow and needed his lungs.

qa.q: Why was Zubin's heart still racing on the bus?
qa.a: He was nervous about refusing older boys and worried he had sounded stupid, even though he stood firm.

qa.q: What made Zubin's refusal effective?
qa.a: He gave a short, confident reason tied to something he cared about, and Jahnavi gave him an easy way to leave.

qa.q: How might the older boy see Zubin's no?
qa.a: He shrugged it off, which suggests a clear, calm refusal didn't cause a big fight or make Zubin a target.

grounding: It shows a teen at a sports club trip refusing a vape offered by older peers using a rehearsed reason.

passage:
Dear Bhupen,
I'm writing because at Neha's party you saw me refuse that drink, and afterwards you asked how I did it without looking uncool. The truth? I practised. After my cousin got into trouble with alcohol last year, my mother and I sat down and practised things to say. "No thanks, I'm good." "My parents pick me up and they'll know." "I've got a game tomorrow." It felt silly in the kitchen. But at the party, when that boy pushed the cup at me twice, the words came out without thinking. My hands were shaking, but my voice wasn't.
You don't have to explain yourself to anyone. Just have a line ready. And stand near the snacks, it helps 🙂
Tanuja

qa.q: What lines did Tanuja practise in the kitchen?
qa.a: "No thanks, I'm good," "My parents pick me up and they'll know," and "I've got a game tomorrow."

qa.q: What does Tanuja's shaking hands but steady voice suggest?
qa.a: Tanuja felt nervous and pressured inside, but the practice helped Tanuja sound calm and firm on the outside.

qa.q: What is the most useful advice in Tanuja's letter?
qa.a: Having a ready line practised in advance means you don't have to think under pressure, and you don't owe anyone an explanation.

qa.q: How might Bhupen feel after reading the letter?
qa.a: Bhupen may feel relieved that refusing isn't about being naturally confident, and more ready to try it.

grounding: A teen's letter explains rehearsing refusal lines for when alcohol is offered by peers.

passage: You're asking about the joint thing? Okay. I'm Pallavi. It was at my friend's farmhouse last summer. Someone passed a rolled joint around the circle, and everyone was laughing. I watched it come closer, like a slow train. I didn't want it. I'd read about how it messes with teenage brains, and my uncle had problems with drugs, so I'd seen the other side. But I also didn't want to be the weird one. My friend Anirban was sitting next to me. When it reached him, he just said, "Pass," and handed it on without a speech. Nobody cared. When it came to me, I said, "Pass," too. That was it. Honestly, I'm grateful he went first.

qa.q: Where was the gathering where the joint was passed around?
qa.a: It was at Pallavi's friend's farmhouse last summer.

qa.q: Why was Pallavi torn when the joint came closer?
qa.a: Pallavi didn't want to use it because of knowing the risks and seeing an uncle struggle, but also feared being seen as the weird one.

qa.q: What made Anirban's refusal easy to copy?
qa.a: He said a single word, "Pass," without a speech, which showed refusing could be simple and not a big scene.

qa.q: How might Anirban feel knowing his "Pass" helped Pallavi?
qa.a: He might be surprised, since it felt small to him, but glad that it made it easier for his friend to say no.

grounding: A teen recounts seeing a friend refuse a drug calmly and following his example.

passage: I'm Lakshmi, Sangeeta's cousin. At my sister's wedding in Coimbatore, the older boys had a table behind the tent with bottles hidden under a tablecloth. I saw one of them wave Sangeeta over. She's sixteen. He poured something into a paper cup and held it out, laughing. She shook her head and held up the lime soda already in her hand. I couldn't hear everything, but I caught, 'No thanks, I'm on dance duty, need my feet.' He pushed the cup closer. She laughed, said it again, and walked off to the dance floor without looking back. Later I asked if she was okay. She shrugged and said, 'I practised saying that in the mirror.' I don't know if she was nervous. She didn't look it.

qa.q: What was Sangeeta holding when the cup was offered?
qa.a: A lime soda.

qa.q: How can you tell Sangeeta felt ready for such a moment?
qa.a: She seemed confident and prepared: she had practised her refusal line in the mirror, then laughed and walked off without looking back.

qa.q: What made Sangeeta's refusal effective?
qa.a: She had a ready, light reason, repeated it calmly when pushed and then walked away.

qa.q: What might the boy with the cup have thought when she walked off?
qa.a: He may have been surprised she didn't give in and realised pushing wasn't going to work.

grounding: An observer sees a teen refuse alcohol at a wedding using a rehearsed line.

passage: Monday: Behind the school canteen, two seniors were passing around a vape. One held it out to Jomon, fifteen. 'Try it, it's just flavour, mango.' Jomon's face went hot. 'Maybe later,' he mumbled and left, feeling like a coward. Wednesday: At the bus stop he told Avni. She didn't laugh. 'Those things still mess with your lungs, flavour or not. And later means they'll ask again.' They made up lines. 'Nah, I've got football.' 'Not my thing.' Jomon repeated them, feeling silly, then less silly. Friday: The senior held it out again. 'Mango, bro.' 'Nah, not my thing. Football.' Jomon kept walking. Behind him, he heard, 'Whatever.' That was it. His heart was pounding, but he grinned all the way to the field.

qa.q: What flavour did the senior say the vape was?
qa.a: Mango.

qa.q: Why did Jomon feel like a coward on Monday?
qa.a: He felt ashamed because he hadn't said a clear no, only mumbled 'maybe later' and left.

qa.q: What helped Jomon refuse more easily on Friday?
qa.a: Rehearsing short, ready lines with Avni so he didn't have to think on the spot.

qa.q: How might Avni feel when Jomon tells her about Friday?
qa.a: She would likely be happy and proud that the lines they practised worked. 😊

grounding: Over several days a teen learns the risk of vaping and rehearses refusing a peer's offer.

passage:
Mohit, you're fifteen now, and one day someone will offer you a cigarette behind the school wall. Let your Lokesh Chacha tell you what happened to me.
I was fifteen too, in Jaipur. Three boys from my class were smoking behind the bus stand. One held out a cigarette. “Just one puff. Don't be a baby.”
My heart was banging. I'd practised a line with my cousin, so I said it: “No, man. Coach will smell it and drop me from the team.” They laughed, but they let it go.
One of those boys, Rakesh, was smoking a packet a day by nineteen. He tried to stop many times.
Have your line ready before anyone asks, Mohit. It's easier than thinking of one on the spot.

qa.q: What line did young Lokesh use to refuse?
qa.a: “No, man. Coach will smell it and drop me from the team.”

qa.q: How did young Lokesh feel when offered the cigarette?
qa.a: He felt nervous, his heart banging, under pressure from the boys.

qa.q: What choice inside the story helped Lokesh refuse?
qa.a: Practising a refusal line beforehand with his cousin, so he could use it under pressure.

qa.q: How might Rakesh have felt when he tried to stop smoking later?
qa.a: He probably felt frustrated and stuck, finding it hard to quit.

grounding: An uncle tells his nephew how a rehearsed refusal helped him say no to smoking at fifteen.

passage:
At the birthday party in a friend's flat in Gurgaon, the music was loud, and Devika's father wasn't coming to pick her up till eleven.
On the balcony, two older boys were passing around a vape. One held it out to her. “Try. It's just flavour, like mango.”
Devika, sixteen, felt everyone look at her. Her friend Shalini nudged her.
She'd practised this. “No thanks, I've got a match tomorrow,” she said, and turned to Shalini. “Come, let's get cake.”
Inside, she texted her father: Can you come at 9:30 instead? I'll explain.
He arrived at 9:25. In the car she told him everything. He said, “You handled that well. Thank you for telling me.”

qa.q: What did the boy say the vape was like?
qa.a: He said it's just flavour, like mango.

qa.q: How did Devika feel when everyone looked at her on the balcony?
qa.a: She felt pressured and uneasy, but prepared to refuse.

qa.q: What steps helped Devika stay safe?
qa.a: Using a practised refusal line, moving away with Shalini and texting her father to pick her up early.

qa.q: How did Devika's father respond when she told him?
qa.a: He came early, listened and thanked her for telling him.

grounding: At a party a sixteen-year-old refuses a vape with a rehearsed line and asks her father to come early.

passage:
At the college fest in Pune, Aparna, seventeen, and her friend Tenzin were watching the band when a group of seniors called them over. A cooler of beer was open on the grass.
“Here, juniors.” A can was held out.
Aparna had thought about this moment. She'd read about how alcohol affects the body at her age, and she didn't want to feel out of control somewhere unfamiliar.
“I'm good, thanks,” she said, raising her lemon soda. “Band's amazing, na?”
The senior shrugged. “Suit yourself.”
Tenzin, who had reached for a can, paused, then put it back. “Me too. I've got practice at six.”
They walked back to the front of the crowd. Nobody asked again.

qa.q: What was Aparna holding when she refused?
qa.a: A lemon soda.

qa.q: How might Aparna have felt when the can was held out?
qa.a: She probably felt a little nervous but confident, having thought about this moment beforehand.

qa.q: What made Aparna's refusal effective?
qa.a: She said no politely, raised her own drink and changed the subject, so it wasn't a big deal.

qa.q: How might Tenzin have been affected by Aparna's refusal?
qa.a: Seeing her say no made it easier for Tenzin to refuse too.

grounding: A seventeen-year-old understands the risks of alcohol and refuses it easily at a college fest.

passage:
At my cousin's wedding last winter, the boys were passing a bottle behind the tent. My cousin Rafiq waved me over. "Minakshi! Try a sip. It's a wedding!"
I was fifteen. I wanted to look grown-up. My hand almost reached out.
Then I remembered my uncle at the last wedding, who couldn't stand and shouted at his wife in front of everyone. And the leaflet from school: drinking young affects your growing brain.
"No. I'll get a cold drink," I said.
Rafiq rolled his eyes. "So boring."
"Boring and I can remember the dance." I went back and danced with my Nani.
Rafiq came to find me later. He looked green. I kind of felt sorry for him.

qa.q: Where were the boys passing a bottle?
qa.a: Behind the tent.

qa.q: What was Minakshi feeling when her hand almost reached out?
qa.a: Minakshi felt tempted and pressured, wanting to look grown-up.

qa.q: What helped Minakshi say no?
qa.a: Remembering Minakshi's uncle at the last wedding and what she'd learnt about alcohol and the growing brain.

qa.q: How might Rafiq be feeling when he comes to find Minakshi?
qa.a: Rafiq probably feels unwell and maybe a little regretful.

grounding: A young person recalls refusing alcohol at a wedding using what Minakshi knew about the risks.

passage:
Hockey coach's note, U-16 team.
Today behind the pavilion, two seniors offered Anand a packet of gutka. I was close enough to see and hear.
Anand said, "No, bhaiya. My dadaji chewed that. He lost his teeth and his voice." They laughed. He didn't move. "No." Then he walked back to the field.
Nandini, who had seen it too, walked with him. I heard her say, "That was brave."
I spoke to the seniors this afternoon and informed the school. Tomorrow I'll talk to the whole team about tobacco and how to refuse, and I'll mention, without naming him, that someone did it well today. — Coach Fernandes

qa.q: What did the seniors offer Anand?
qa.a: A packet of gutka.

qa.q: What was Anand feeling when he refused?
qa.a: Anand felt firm and determined, remembering what happened to his dadaji.

qa.q: What did Coach Fernandes do after seeing this?
qa.a: He spoke to the seniors, informed the school and planned a team talk on refusing tobacco.

qa.q: How does Nandini see Anand's refusal?
qa.a: Nandini sees it as brave and shows support by walking with him.

grounding: A coach notes a teen refusing tobacco from seniors and follows up.

passage:
Friday
Lokesh's diary. Today behind the sports shed, Kashish pulled out a vape pen that smelled like mango. "Try, it's not even smoking. It's just flavour."
I actually wanted to. Everyone was standing around laughing. But I remembered what we'd practised in life-skills class: say no, give a short reason, change the subject, walk away if needed. It sounded so fake in class. Today it wasn't.
I said, "Nah, I've got a match tomorrow and I need my lungs." Kashish rolled their eyes. "Boring." I said, "Yeah, boring and breathing. Anyone coming for samosas?" Two people came with me.
My heart was pounding the whole way to the canteen. But I didn't feel stupid. I felt kind of strong.

qa.q: What did the vape pen smell like?
qa.a: It smelled like mango.

qa.q: How did Lokesh feel after walking away?
qa.a: Lokesh felt nervous, with a pounding heart, but also strong and not stupid.

qa.q: Why did the rehearsed refusal work?
qa.a: A short no with a reason, then changing the subject and walking away gave Lokesh a ready script, and even brought two others along.

qa.q: How might the two people who came for samosas have felt?
qa.a: They may have felt relieved to have an easy way out of the pressure too.

grounding: Shows a teen using a rehearsed refusal when offered a vape by a peer.

passage:
At the bus stand of their small town, a group of older boys was passing round a packet of gutka. One of them held it out to Imran. "Try it, it keeps you awake for exams."
Imran felt his face go hot. They were his cousin's friends. Saying no felt rude.
Bidisha, waiting for the same bus, didn't look up from her book. "His uncle's teeth are ruined from that stuff," she said. "And his mouth has sores. Ask him."
The boy laughed. "Who asked you?"
Imran took a breath. "She's right. I've seen it. No thanks." He stepped back.
When the bus came he sat next to Bidisha. "Thanks."
"You said the no," she said. "I just helped a bit."
That evening he told his mother, just so she knew the offer had happened.

qa.q: What did the older boy say gutka does?
qa.a: He said it keeps you awake for exams.

qa.q: Why did saying no feel hard for Imran?
qa.a: Imran felt embarrassed and nervous, because the boys were his cousin's friends and refusing felt rude.

qa.q: What would you advise a teen in Imran's place next time?
qa.a: Give a short, firm "No thanks" with a real reason, step away, and tell a trusted adult if the offers continue.

qa.q: How might Bidisha have felt speaking up to the older boys?
qa.a: Bidisha may have felt a little nervous, but protective and confident enough to back up Imran.

grounding: Shows a teen refusing tobacco from older peers, supported by a friend, and telling a parent.

The party in Nour's backyard in Leeds was loud and warm, fairy lights strung across the fence. Abebe, sixteen, was by the snack table when an older boy held out a vape. "Go on. Mango flavour. Everyone's having one."
Abebe's heart thumped. A few people turned to watch.
He and Nour had joked about this exact moment on the bus last week, practising lines like a silly play.
"Nah, I'm good, mate," Abebe said, easy, and picked up a lemonade instead. "Got a football trial Saturday."
"One won't kill you."
"Still no." He turned back to Nour. "You said you'd show me that new song?"
The older boy shrugged and moved on. Nour grinned and bumped his shoulder. "Smooth. Just like we practised."

qa.a: He said it was mango flavour.

qa.q: What was Abebe feeling when people turned to watch?
qa.a: Abebe felt nervous, his heart thumping, and under pressure with others watching.

qa.q: What helped Abebe refuse without a big scene?
qa.a: He had practised lines with Nour, kept his no short and friendly, gave a simple reason, and changed the subject.
